reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / WHO guidance
clinicalPearls: A flavivirus transmitted by Ixodes ticks across endemic parts of Europe and Asia, with European, Siberian, and Far Eastern subtypes of differing severity
The illness is classically biphasic: an initial viraemic flu-like phase, a symptom-free interval of about a week, then a second neurological phase with meningitis, encephalitis, or myelitis
An important additional route is consumption of unpasteurised milk or dairy products from infected goats, sheep, or cattle (alimentary transmission)
The Far Eastern subtype tends to cause more severe monophasic disease with higher mortality and sequelae, while the European subtype more often shows the classic biphasic pattern
Neurological sequelae such as cognitive impairment, ataxia, and flaccid paralysis (especially of the shoulder girdle) can be long-lasting
There is no specific antiviral; management is supportive, and an effective inactivated vaccine is the mainstay of prevention for residents and travellers to endemic areas
Diagnosis is usually serological (IgM and IgG in serum and cerebrospinal fluid), as viraemia and detectable RNA have often cleared by the neurological phase
reference.pathophysiology: Tick-borne encephalitis virus is inoculated during the bite of an infected Ixodes tick, or ingested in unpasteurised dairy products. It first replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing the initial viraemic phase with nonspecific febrile symptoms. In a proportion of patients the virus subsequently crosses the blood-brain barrier and infects neurons, particularly in the brainstem, cerebellum, and anterior horns of the spinal cord, provoking an inflammatory meningoencephalitis or myelitis. By the time neurological disease appears, viraemia has typically resolved and the host antibody response is detectable, which is why diagnosis is largely serological.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex virus and other viral encephalitides
West Nile virus and other flaviviral neuroinvasive disease
Guillain-Barre syndrome when flaccid paralysis predominates
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM and IgG serology for tick-borne encephalitis virus
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord for thalamic, cerebellar, brainstem, or anterior-horn involvement
RT-PCR on blood during the early viraemic phase, recognising it is often negative by the neurological phase
Testing for co-transmitted Lyme borreliosis given shared Ixodes vectors
Electrophysiology when myelitis or peripheral involvement is suspected
redFlags: Declining consciousness or brainstem signs indicating severe encephalitis
Flaccid limb or respiratory-muscle weakness from myelitis
Rapidly progressive monophasic course suggesting a more severe viral subtype
reference.prognosis: Many patients recover fully, but a substantial minority, especially with the Siberian or Far Eastern subtypes or with encephalitic or myelitic involvement, are left with persistent neurological sequelae, and mortality is highest with the Far Eastern subtype.
pitfalls: Discharging a patient during the afebrile interval and missing the second neurological phase
Relying on RT-PCR in the neurological phase, when serology is the appropriate test
Overlooking alimentary transmission from unpasteurised dairy products
Failing to consider co-infection with Lyme borreliosis from the same tick exposure
Not offering vaccination to at-risk residents and travellers as prevention
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
World Health Organization tick-borne encephalitis position paper
management: Provide supportive care, since there is no specific antiviral, with analgesia, antipyretics and fluid and electrolyte management
Prevent disease with the inactivated tick-borne encephalitis vaccine for residents of and travellers to endemic areas, alongside tick-bite avoidance and avoiding unpasteurised dairy products
Manage severe encephalitic or myelitic disease in critical care, with ventilatory support for bulbar or respiratory involvement and control of raised intracranial pressure and seizures
Monitor neurological status, swallowing and airway safety through the illness
Arrange neurorehabilitation for lasting sequelae such as cognitive impairment, ataxia and flaccid paralysis
Test for co-transmitted Lyme borreliosis given the shared Ixodes vector, and treat if confirmed
